meta.blurb: Kofi has wished for years to make pottery, and nothing has happened. With help from Ana, a retired mountain guide, he turns a wish into a goal with a date, a plan and a price. Follow six months of real progress, slumps and all.
meta.bible: Kofi Mensah: a twenty-nine-year-old accountant who dreams of making Pottery; thoughtful, careful with numbers, afraid of looking foolish. Ana Silva: his neighbour, sixty-six, a retired mountain guide of thirty years, plain-spoken and kind; she turns groups back when the weather is bad. Joy Bell: the teacher of a beginners' class at the community Studio, cheerful and honest. Dan: Kofi's friend. Riverside Market: the town market where Kofi sells on the last Saturday of June. The goal: sell twenty Mugs that Kofi made himself before the thirtieth of June, about twenty-six weeks from the first of January; he sells sixteen. Five hours a week: Tuesday and Thursday evenings and Saturday morning. Key terms: Wish, Goal, Deadline, Milestone, Clay, Glaze, Kiln, Wheel, Tally, Obstacle, Review. Real research, mentioned carefully: psychologists have found over several decades that specific, challenging goals tend to bring better results than vague ones; plans in an if-then form have helped many people follow through; imagining obstacles as well as success may help in some studies; the effect of telling others about a goal is mixed. No other studies or numbers are invented. This is original practical self-help for adults, one idea in each beat, building to a final takeaway. Voice and tone: warm, concrete, encouraging, never bossy.

C1C2: Kofi Mensah spent his days among spreadsheets and his evenings among daydreams, and the favourite of these was a small workshop where he made pottery with his own hands. Every January he promised himself that this would be the year, and every December he found himself in exactly the same chair with exactly the same dream. Somewhere, he suspected, there must be a difference between the people who wish and the people who do.

On the first of January, Kofi found his neighbour Ana Silva repotting herbs in the courtyard, and out of nowhere he told her about his dream. Ana had spent thirty years guiding people up mountains, and she listened with the attentive stillness of someone who has heard many dreams. A wish, she said at last, is a fine thing to have, but it is not yet a goal.

A wish is like a cloud on the horizon, Ana explained, pleasant to look at and impossible to walk toward, because it has no edges. A goal, by contrast, has a finish line, a point at which anyone could look at the result and say honestly that it was reached or that it was not. Turning one into the other, she said, is the first and most important piece of all mountaineering.

Wishes stay wishes, Ana said, for three simple reasons: they have no date, they have no first step, and they ask nothing of you today. Because tomorrow always seems a perfectly good time to begin, a dream can wait politely for decades. The remedy is to give it a deadline and a first step, and to start paying the price before it feels comfortable.

Kofi sat at his kitchen table and wrote down every goal he had ever half-held, and the list grew to nine: pottery, Spanish, a marathon, a garden, a book, a better bicycle, and three more. Ana looked over his shoulder and observed that someone who chases nine rabbits rarely catches even one. Her advice was to choose a single goal for the next six months and to put the rest gently in a drawer.

Ana's test for choosing was simple: imagine yourself a year from today, and ask which goal you would be saddest to have ignored. Kofi closed his eyes, thought about it for a full minute, and found that pottery was the only one that made his chest ache. He circled it, slid the other eight strips into a drawer, and felt an unexpected lightness, as though he had put down eight heavy bags.

A goal without a reason, Ana said, is like a tent without pegs: it looks fine until the first strong wind arrives. She asked Kofi why he truly wanted to make pottery, and his first answers, such as money and fun, did not satisfy either of them. After a long pause he said that he wanted to make something real that people could hold, because his work all day consisted of numbers on a screen.

She asked him to write the reason on a card in a single sentence, and then to test it by imagining that nobody would ever know, applaud or buy anything. If the goal still seemed worth the trouble, the reason was strong, but if it faded, it probably belonged to someone else's expectations. Kofi's card said that he wanted to make things people can hold, and it passed the test.

Wanting to make pottery was still a cloud, so Ana helped him sharpen it into something with edges. After several drafts, Kofi wrote on a large sheet of paper that he would sell twenty mugs, all made by his own hands, before the thirtieth of June. The sentence frightened him slightly, which Ana said was a good sign, since a goal that frightens you a little is probably worth having.

Ana, who loved to read, told him that psychologists have studied goal setting for several decades. Over and over, they have found that people given a specific, challenging target tend to perform better than people who are simply told to do their best, although no rule works perfectly for everyone. A vague aim, it seems, lets us quietly excuse ourselves at every single step along the way.

A good goal can be counted, Ana said, because you cannot steer by a feeling that changes with the weather. Kofi drew a row of twenty small boxes on the sheet, one for every mug he planned to sell, and decided that he would fill them in with a bright pen as the weeks went by. The simple picture made the distance between where he stood and where he wished to be visible at a glance.

Ana described the sweet spot as a goal that stretches you without snapping you. If the target is too easy, it fails to excite the mind, and if it is far too large, the mind quietly refuses to take it seriously. Twenty mugs in six months, for a beginner with a full-time job, was ambitious but plausible, and she nodded her approval.

A goal without a date, Ana said, is a hope in a nice coat. Kofi circled the thirtieth of June on his wall calendar, counted back to the present, and found about twenty-six weeks, which felt both generous and alarmingly short. The date turned a dream into a stretch of real days, each of which could now be used or wasted.

Ana told him that a goal kept in the head is easily bullied by the day, so Kofi copied his sentence, his reason and his twenty boxes onto one sheet. He taped it to the bathroom mirror, where it greeted him twice a day and made it very difficult to pretend that he had forgotten. Every time he brushed his teeth, he was quietly reminded of what he had promised.

Ana sketched a mountain on the back of an envelope and marked a row of small tents along the path. Nobody, she told him, climbs a peak in one stretch, so a guide breaks the route into camps, each one close enough to be reached before dark. A big goal should be broken down in the same way, so that every stage feels like a day's walk and not like an impossible cliff.

Ana taught him to plan backward, starting from the finish and asking what must be true a month before it, then a month before that. By the time Kofi reached January, he had a list: learn to make a mug, make a first batch, make a better batch, then find a market and book a stall. The plan was not perfect, but it was real, and it fitted onto a single page.

The first camp on his route was simply to learn, so Kofi enrolled in a beginners' class at the community studio on Tuesday evenings. The teacher, Joy Bell, welcomed the class with a cheerful warning that everybody's first pots look something like melted candles, and that this was entirely normal. He sat down at the wheel, covered his hands in wet clay, and felt happier than he had in months.

Ana's favourite rule was that you should always know your very next action, however tiny it might be. A vague note such as work on pottery wastes energy, she said, whereas a precise note such as book the studio for Saturday morning can be carried out at once. Kofi ended every work session by writing the next step on a sticky note, and he began each new session by reading it.

Ana then taught him a trick that researchers call an if-then plan: you decide in advance exactly when and where you will act, so that the moment itself triggers the action. Kofi wrote that if it was Saturday at nine, then he would be at the studio, and he placed his apron by the front door. In a number of studies, plans of this kind have helped people follow through, though they are certainly no magic.

Ana had once turned a group back from a mountain because of fog, and she said that the best guides spend as much time imagining storms as imagining summits. Kofi was asked to picture his success vividly, and then to picture, just as clearly, whatever might get in the way. Some research suggests that this combination helps people prepare, whereas dreaming of success alone can make them relax too soon.

Kofi listed what would probably stop him: tiredness after long days at the office, the cost of clay and studio time, and the fear of making ugly pots in front of strangers. Beside each obstacle he wrote an answer, such as a ten-minute rest before class, a monthly budget, and a promise to treat every bad pot as a lesson. When trouble came, he would already have a calm, sensible plan waiting for it.

Time, Ana said, is never found but always taken, so Kofi looked closely at an ordinary week and decided where he would take it from. Two evenings and one Saturday morning added up to about five hours, and he blocked them in his diary as though they were meetings with an important client. The television, he noticed with a small smile, would simply have to forgive him.

Being an accountant, Kofi enjoyed this stage more than he admitted: he added up lessons, clay, glaze, firing fees and the cost of a market stall, and divided the total into monthly amounts. A small jar on the shelf received its share on every payday, which meant that money would never become the excuse for stopping. Knowing the exact price of a dream, he found, makes it far less frightening.

Joy Bell explained that practice is most useful when it is aimed at the part you find hardest, not at the part that already feels comfortable. Kofi's walls kept collapsing, so for three weeks he made nothing but tall wobbly cylinders, over and over, until the clay began to obey his fingers. It was dull and repetitive work, but it was the quickest way forward that he could find.

Ana had always insisted that progress needs a mirror, so Kofi asked Joy to judge one of his mugs without softening the truth. She turned it slowly in her hands and told him, kindly but plainly, that the base was too thick and the handle too small for a grown-up finger. It hurt a little, but it was precisely the information he could not have seen alone.

Beside the twenty empty boxes, Kofi taped a second chart on which he placed a coloured dot after every practice session. Within a month the dots had formed a satisfying little crowd, and he discovered that the mere sight of progress made him reluctant to break the pattern. The chart was not clever, but it showed him, every morning, that he was a person who turned up.

Ana pointed out a quiet difficulty: Kofi could not control whether strangers would buy his mugs, but he could completely control how often he practised and how carefully he worked. She therefore asked him to add small process goals, such as two evening sessions and one long Saturday every week, to the larger target. Effort that you control is the surest road toward results that you do not.

By March the early excitement had drained away, the mugs still looked clumsy, and the finish seemed to be a very long way off. Ana had seen the same dip on every mountain, she said, because the beginning is thrilling and the ending is exciting, but the long middle is only walking. Everyone feels it, and the people who reach the top are simply those who keep walking.

When motivation fails, Ana said, do not argue with it; shrink the task until it is almost laughably easy. Kofi promised himself just ten minutes at the wheel on his worst evenings, and the trick worked more often than he expected, because beginning is nearly always harder than continuing. Even on the days when ten minutes was all he did, the dot still went on the chart.

In April, Kofi caught a heavy cold and missed nine days of practice, and a gloomy voice in his head announced that the whole project was ruined. Ana disagreed warmly: a lost week is a bend in the path, not the end of it, and the real danger lies in the second miss and the third. He returned to the studio on a Tuesday with a rusty hand and a rather grateful heart.

Kofi asked Ana whether she would meet him once a month, simply to ask how the goal was going and to listen to his honest answer. The knowledge that someone would be asking made him want to have something real to report, and it gave his progress an audience of one. Ana, who had always disliked guiding people alone, agreed with obvious and open pleasure.

Kofi told his friend Dan the whole plan, including the date, the numbers and the steps, and Dan promised to ask about it every few weeks. Ana added a cautionary note: some studies suggest that announcing a dream can bring a pleasant feeling of progress too early, although the research is mixed. The safe course, she said, is to share the plan and the work, and not only the dream.

Ana reminded him that the surroundings can make a first step easy or hard, so Kofi cleared a corner of his flat and set up a small table with his tools, a damp cloth and a covered bucket of clay. When everything was ready and in sight, starting took ten seconds instead of ten excuses. It cost him a little floor space, but it saved him a great deal of resistance.

In May, a glossy advertisement for a language course nearly tempted Kofi away from the wheel, since fresh ideas always look brighter than the old, familiar work. Remembering the nine rabbits, he wrote the idea on a list titled after June and closed the laptop firmly. A new goal, he reminded himself, is a perfectly good reward for finishing the old one.

On Sunday evenings Kofi sat down with a notebook for ten minutes and answered three questions in writing: what had gone well, what had got in the way, and which three steps mattered most in the coming week. It was less like a lecture and more like a quiet conversation with the person he was becoming. Over the months, the notebook became a map of where his time had really gone.

At the halfway point, Ana suggested a pause to ask a difficult question: whether the goal still felt worth chasing, or whether it was merely habit. Kofi read his card, thought about the hours he had spent at the wheel, and discovered that he wanted the goal even more than he had in January. It is a strange sort of comfort, he told her, to be sure for a second time.

When Kofi counted honestly, he had only six mugs of a quality he would be proud to sell, and he was well behind the pace he needed. Ana taught him the golden rule of the mountains: if the route is not working, change the route, and keep the summit. He added an extra Saturday session to every week and trimmed one evening of television from his life.

In May, Kofi opened the cooled kiln with high hopes, and his heart sank as he found four of his best mugs split by long, clean cracks. Joy was sympathetic but unsurprised, explaining that pots crack for many reasons, such as trapped air bubbles or drying unevenly, and that every potter loses some. Failure, she said, is simply the clay's way of giving information that you can use.

That night Kofi wondered seriously whether he should stop, and the idea felt almost like relief. In the morning, however, he read the card on his mirror, and the old sentence about making things that people can hold seemed as true as ever. Four broken mugs had taught him something valuable about clay, but they had not changed in the least what he truly wanted.

By the end of May, Kofi had ten mugs that he was proud to put on a shelf, and he took Dan out for dinner to mark the occasion. Ana had always maintained that celebration is not a distraction from the work but part of its engine, since the mind returns gladly to whatever it has learned to enjoy. He raised his glass to the first ten, and to the ten still to come.

One evening Kofi browsed photographs of a famous potter's flawless shelves and felt his confidence trickle away. Ana, who had heard the same worry from many climbers, reminded him that he was comparing his own first year with someone else's twentieth. The only fair comparison, she said, is between the person you are now and the person you were when you began.

Dan bought the first blue mug and insisted on paying the full price, even though Kofi tried to give it to him as a gift. That evening, Kofi coloured the first box of the twenty on his bathroom sheet, and the tiny bright rectangle gave him a happiness out of all proportion to its size. A goal that had been a cloud in January was now a real, countable thing.

Kofi booked a stall at the Riverside Market for the last Saturday of June and wrote a long checklist of everything that might be needed, from a cash box and a table cloth to a sign with prices. He wrapped each mug carefully in newspaper and practised saying the price aloud in front of the mirror, which felt ridiculous and helped enormously. Preparation, Ana said, is the cheapest and most reliable kind of courage that a person can buy.

On the last Saturday of June, Kofi stood behind his stall in the early sunshine, smiling at every passer-by with a mixture of terror and hope. By lunchtime he had sold nine mugs, and he began to notice what people actually liked: the larger handles, the deep blue glaze, and the small mugs for children. Each sale was a tiny lesson, delivered by a stranger who would never know it.

By the end of the market day, Kofi had sold eleven mugs, and together with the five that friends and colleagues had bought earlier, his total reached sixteen. On the thirtieth of June he stood in front of the bathroom mirror and counted four empty boxes, and for a moment the disappointment was sharp. Then he remembered that in January he had owned a wish, and now he owned sixteen real sales.

Ana poured the tea and said that a missed target is data, not a verdict, and she asked him to look at the chart as a scientist would. The cracked batch had cost him four mugs, almost exactly the gap, and selling to friends and colleagues had worked better than he had dared to hope. A goal that is nearly reached, she added, has still carried you a very long way from where you started.

Kofi did not hesitate for long before taking a clean sheet of paper and writing a new sentence at the top: forty mugs sold by the end of December, helped by a small online page. He added a reason, a set of milestones and a list of obstacles, which now took about twenty minutes instead of a month. Goals, he realised, are built one on top of another, each stage standing on the last.

Ana showed Kofi a photograph of a snowy peak that hung by her door, and she told him that she had once turned back only a short climb from its summit because the weather had changed. It was one of the best decisions of her life, she said, because the goal was never to stand on the top but to have a good life of climbing. She returned the following year, in clear weather, and that summit was sweeter than any other.

One evening in autumn, Kofi stood in front of his shelf of mugs, each one a little better than the one before it, and thought about the person who had sat dreaming in a chair twelve months earlier. He was the same man, with the same job and the same flat, but his relationship with his dreams had changed completely. He no longer waited for the right moment to wish; he built the moment with his own hands.

Here is the whole lesson in a few lines: choose a single goal that matters, make it specific and countable, and give it a reason and a date. Break it into stages, plan for the obstacles, check your progress every week, and treat every setback as information rather than a verdict. Then begin today, because a goal that sticks is simply a wish that someone decided to take seriously.
